abstract: Significance Translation and its machinery appear to be key players in pathophysiological processes. In particular, translational factors have been implicated in cell identity change, such as during epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT). However, it remains to be determined whether ribosome components also contribute to the change in cellular identity. Here, we have shown that a single ribosomal protein is responsible for EMT. Not only are ribosome composition and translation modulated during EMT, but overexpression of RPL36A is sufficient to trigger the acquisition of mesenchymal characteristics. This work demonstrates the existence of heterogeneity in ribosome composition during cell identity change and the unique role of a single ribosomal protein in controlling cell identity.
methods:
Materials and Methods
Cellular Models and Viral Infection.
hMEC line (Lonza Bioscience, CC-2551) and its derivates were cultured in DMEM F12 media (Gibco, 21331020) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (Capricorn Scientific, FBS-12A), 1% penicillin–streptomycin, 0.01 µg/mL hEGF, 0.5 µg/mL hydrocortisone, and 280 mU/mL insulin at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere with 5% CO
2
. MCF10A (ATCC, CRL-10317™) cells were cultured in DMEM F12 media (Gibco, 21331020) supplemented with 5% horse serum (Gibco, 16050122), 1% penicillin–streptomycin, 1X GlutaMax, 2 mM L-Glutamine (Gibco, 25030024), 0.02 µg/mL hEGF, 0.5 µg/mL hydrocortisone, 300 mU/mL insulin, and 100 ng/mL cholera toxin at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere with 5% CO
2
.
Ribosome Profiling and tRNAome.
5.10
7
and 5.10
6
hMEC-derived cells were used for RIBOseq and RNAseq, respectively. Stranded Total RNA library preparation kit respectively (Illumina) and next generation sequencing was performed using a Next Seq single read 75. Data were analyzed using the Ribodoc package (
SI Appendix
,
Materials and Methods
). tRNAome has been realized by Arraystar Inc.
Readthrough Luciferase Reporter Assays.
The pAC18 plasmid (
29
) contains a nonsense mutation (UGA) flanked by two F2A self-cleavage sites that separate the luciferase and β-galactosidase coding phases. β-galactosidase and luciferase activities were assayed using Glo lysis buffer (Promega). Readthrough efficacy was estimated by calculating the ratio of luciferase activity to β-galactosidase activity obtained with the mutant construct, with normalization against an in-frame wild-type control construct.
Ribosome Purification.
Cytoplasmic fractions were obtained by mechanical lysis of cells using the PreCellys device (Ozyme) and centrifugation at 750
g
for 10 min to pellet nuclei then 12,000
g
for 10 min to pellet mitochondria (
32
). Cytoplasmic fractions were loaded onto a 1 M sucrose cushion in buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4; 5 mM MgCl
2
; 500 mM KCl; 2 mM DTT) and centrifuged for 2 h at 250,000
g
. Ribosome pellets were resuspended in buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4; 5 mM MgCl
2
; 25 mM KCl).
MS-Based Quantitative Proteomic Analysis of Ribosomal Fractions.
Five biological replicates of ribosomes were purified from hMEC and hMEC-ZEB1 cell lines before characterization by MS-based proteomic analysis. Only proteins quantified in at least 5 replicates of 1 condition were kept. For each sample, individual iBAQ values were normalized by the sum of iBAQ values coming from ribosomal proteins. Differentially expressed proteins were sorted out using a log2(fold change) cutoff of 1 and an adjusted
P
-value cutoff of 0.005, allowing to reach an FDR threshold of 1% according to the Benjamini–Hochberg estimator.
Immunofluorescence.
Cells were grown on glass coverslips and fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde in 1X PBS before permeabilization with 0.5% Triton X-100 in 1X PBS. Primary antibodies were applied before secondary antibodies were labeled with AlexaFluor488 or 555 (Molecular Probes) (
SI Appendix
, Table S1
). Coverslips were mounted using the Fluoromount G mounting medium (EMS). Images were acquired on a Zeiss confocal microscope (Zeiss LSM780 NLO), thanks to the Cell Imaging Platform (CRCL, Lyon, France).

body:
The epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) is a dynamic and often reversible process of transdifferentiation that generates mesenchymal cells from epithelial ones (
1
–
3
). Its cellular hallmarks include loss of adhesiveness and cell polarity promoting cell dispersion and the acquisition of a specific cytoskeletal architecture that enhances cell migration and invasion. Despite the contribution of EMT to normal organ physiology during embryogenesis and adulthood, its aberrant reactivation has been reported in different human diseases (
4
).
EMT commitment is driven by deep transcriptional reprogramming coupled to epigenetic events (
1
–
3
). It relies on an intricate network of EMT-inducing transcription factors (EMT-TFs) including the different ZEB (ZEB1 and ZEB2), TWIST (TWIST1 and TWIST2), or SNAIL (SNAIL, SLUG, and SNAI3) families. EMT-TFs were primarily shown to repress
CDH1
(
i.e.
, E-cadherin) transcription and activate
VIM
(
i.e.
, Vimentin), inducing the loss of cell–cell contacts of epithelial cells and the acquisition of motility properties (
5
,
6
). This transcriptional regulation is associated with an epigenetic reprogramming that has been suggested to govern the stability of EMT by defining the residency of cells in a given phenotypic state during the transition (
7
). Although changes in gene expression are the driving force of EMT-induced cell plasticity, few studies have assessed the role of translation in EMT (
3
). It was reported that the reactivation of EMT-TFs and mesenchymal markers at the translational level was sufficient to promote EMT. Indeed, IRES (Internal Ribosome Entry Site)-dependent translation of
LAMB1
or
SNAI1
mRNAs and the specific translation of
Dab2
or
ILEI
mRNAs were shown to trigger EMT (
3
,
8
–
12
). However, translational reprogramming during EMT remains to be characterized.
Increasing evidence supports the notion that components of the translational apparatus can specifically modulate the translation of some mRNAs, thus contributing to the establishment of different pathophysiological phenotypes. For example, the eukaryotic initiation factor eIF3D, which stabilizes the complex integrating the initiator tRNA and the small 40S ribosomal particle, directly regulates the translation of
c-JUN
and
BTG1
mRNAs to modulate cell growth (
13
,
14
). Emerging data also indicate that the ribosome itself is an actor of translational regulation, modulation of ribosome composition contributing to the specific translation of particular mRNA subsets (
15
,
16
). Heterogeneity in ribosome composition has been reported at both ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and protein levels, the latter being one of the most extensively investigated mechanisms. In mice, depletion of RPL38 decreases IRES-dependent translation of
Hoxa9
mRNA and results in the loss of tissue patterning (
17
,
18
). Interestingly, it was reported that increased ribosome biogenesis promotes EMT (
19
). Furthermore, components of the translational apparatus promote EMT, as the acquisition of EMT features is driven by changes in the tRNA repertoire or by decreasing the expression of the canonical eIF3E factor (
20
,
21
).
However, it remains to compare the modulation of transcriptional and translational landscapes in stable epithelial and mesenchymal stages or the associated changes in ribosome composition. Here, using genome-wide approaches we depict the fine-tunings of both translational landscape and machinery that occur during EMT in adult human mammary cells, as well as the role of ribosomal proteins in EMT commitment.
Results
Translational Reprogramming Is as Important as Transcriptional Reprogramming in Specifying the Molecular and Cellular Phenotype of ZEB1-Induced Mesenchymal Cells.
To decipher changes in translation and transcription occurring in mesenchymal cells compared to epithelial ones, we performed ribosome profiling in an isogenic model of human mammary epithelial cells (hMEC) overexpressing or not ZEB1, one of the strongest EMT-TF drivers (
22
). As previously described, ZEB1 overexpression was sufficient to promote a complete switch in both cell morphology and EMT-related molecular features (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S1
). Using this cellular model, we compared i) steady-state mRNA levels in epithelial and mesenchymal stages, by analyzing total RNA using RNAseq that reflects changes in transcription level, nuclear-cytoplasmic export and mRNA stability, thereafter simply referred to total mRNA level; as well as ii) actively translated mRNA levels, by analyzing ribosome-protected mRNAs using RIBOseq (
i.e.
, ribosome footprinting coupled to RNAseq). As previously shown, RIBOseq data mainly detected the 29-mer motif resulting from the precise mRNA protection by the ribosome, the mapping of which is enriched in mRNA open-reading frames (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S2
A
–
C
) (
23
).
Based on biological replicates, read counts were used to calculate log2 fold-changes (FC) and adjusted
P
-values for RNAseq and RIBOseq data by comparing hMEC-ZEB1 to hMEC. The robustness of RNAseq and RIBOseq log2(FC) values was first verified by comparing them to the ones obtained from polysome profiling (
i.e.
, isolation of mRNAs bound by ribosomes) coupled to medium throughput RT-qPCR, on 90 randomly chosen genes using 5 independent experiments (Spearman correlation: RNAseq,
P
< 0.0001 and r
2
= 0.75; RIBOseq,
P
< 0.0001 and r
2
= 0.78) (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S2
D
–
G
). We then applied different thresholds as detailed in the decision tree to compare changes in levels of total mRNAs (RNAseq) or ribosome-protected mRNAs (RIBOseq) (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S2
H
). Using our approach, three main classes of significantly dysregulated mRNAs were identified (
Fig. 1
A
and
B
and
Dataset S1
).

These three classes had the following characteristics i) total and ribosome-associated levels vary concomitantly (“BOTH”, black); ii) total levels vary independently of ribosome-associated ones (“RNAseq”, green); and iii) ribosome-associated levels vary without change in their total levels (“RIBOseq”, pink). The number of dysregulated mRNA in each class is given (

Hallmark_EMT signature
. Individual log2(FC) of RNAseq or RIBOseq data are shown for the mRNAs belonging to the
Hallmark_EMT signature

First, 1,065 mRNAs were significantly and differentially regulated in hMEC-ZEB1 compared to hMEC using both RNAseq and RIBOseq (
Fig. 1
A
and
B
, “BOTH” class, black). These mRNAs corresponded to a concomitant change in levels of total and ribosome-protected mRNAs, suggesting the coupling of transcription/translation for these mRNAs in ZEB1-induced EMT. This mechanism has already been described as a passive buffer effect, where changes in total mRNA levels mechanically affect levels of mRNA translation (
24
). To determine whether these findings were consistent with EMT, overrepresentation analysis in specific biological pathways was performed. As expected, up-regulated mRNAs mostly represented genes involved in EMT and extracellular matrix organization, while down-regulated mRNAs largely corresponded to genes involved in cell junction, differentiation, and epidermis development (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S3
A
and
Dataset S2
). Overall, the molecular phenotyping data obtained validated the ribosome profiling and were consistent with the extensive transcriptional reprogramming-driven EMT described in the literature (
1
,
2
).
In parallel, up to 2,212 mRNAs show a decoupling between their total and ribosome-protected levels in hMEC-ZEB1 compared to hMEC. These data suggest that these mRNAs are regulated at a translational level in ZEB1-induced EMT. Comparison between RNAseq and RIBOseq methodologies unveiled 179 mRNAs that were either significantly up- or down-regulated exclusively by RNAseq (“RNAseq” class) without change in RIBOseq in hMEC-ZEB1 compared to hMEC, suggesting their regulation at the translational level to maintain a basal rate of translation (
Fig. 1
A
and
B
, green). Moreover, 2,033 mRNAs were significantly modified in hMEC-ZEB1 following the RIBOseq technique, without any change in total mRNA levels (
Fig. 1
A
and
B
, “RIBOseq” class, pink). Thus, in addition to transcriptional reprogramming, translational reprogramming occurs in mesenchymal cells overexpressing ZEB1 compared to epithelial hMEC.
Next, to determine whether mRNAs regulated at the translational level also contribute to the switch in EMT-related cellular processes, we performed overrepresentation analyses focusing either on the “RNAseq” class or on the “RIBOseq” class. However, due to the small sample size in the “RNAseq” class (n = 179), data interpretation was limited (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S3
B
and
Dataset S2
). In contrast, in the “RIBOseq” class, most of the enriched pathways (either significantly up- or down-regulated) reflected those identified in the “BOTH” class and were associated with known EMT-related pathways, such as extracellular matrix or development (
Fig. 1
C
and
SI Appendix
, Fig. S3
A
). Moreover, “RIBOseq” and “BOTH” classes encompassed mRNAs of the
EMT hallmark signature
, including several collagens regulated at either transcriptional or translational level (
Fig. 1
D
). These data suggest that determining EMT commitment from the
EMT hallmark signature
established solely from transcriptomics data must significantly underestimate the level of EMT induced. Finally, some of the top 10 enriched terms were specifically identified in the “RIBOseq” class, such as metabolism of bile acid and inflammation, which correspond to emerging biological functions involved in EMT that could be exploited in the future (
25
–
27
) (
Fig. 1
C
). Overall, these data demonstrate that both transcription and translation contribute to specifying the molecular phenotype of ZEB1-induced mesenchymal cells. Interestingly, the number of mRNAs dysregulated at the translational level was twice as important as the ones dysregulated at the transcriptional level (2,212 vs 1,065, respectively), indicating that translational reprogramming is at least as important as transcriptional reprogramming in EMT.
To rule out the possibility that translational reprogramming associated with EMT is specific to ZEB1, we performed another ribosome profiling in SNAIL-overexpressing hMEC. Similar to ZEB1, SNAIL overexpression was associated with both coupling and uncoupling in transcription/translation (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S4
). Comparison of differentially regulated mRNAs in hMECs overexpressing or not the EMT-TFs, in each of the three main classes (
i.e.
, BOTH, RNAseq, RIBOseq), revealed that some mRNAs are similarly or distinctly regulated by ZEB1 and/or SNAIL at the total or ribosome-protected levels (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S4
). These observations support previous reports at the transcriptional level that ZEB1 and SNAIL both induce EMT, albeit in distinct ways (
1
–
3
). They also demonstrate that the contribution of translational reprogramming in specifying EMT-related cellular processes is not restricted to ZEB1 but is likely a shared feature among EMT-TFs.
Altogether, our data show that translational reprogramming occurs in response to the overexpression of different EMT-TFs and contributes to the molecular and cellular switch occurring in epithelial cells during EMT. Interestingly, we show that translational reprogramming is at least as important as transcriptional reprogramming in ZEB1-induced mesenchymal cells, with approximately 2,000 mRNAs differentially modulated at the translational level.
Ribosomes Display Increased Translational Defects in ZEB1-Induced Mesenchymal Cells.
Having shown that a translational reprogramming occurs in ZEB1-overexpressing mesenchymal cells, we attempted to identify changes in translational fidelity (
i.e.
, accuracy of mRNA decoding during protein synthesis). We used a stop codon readthrough reporter assay allowing us to analyze the recognition of stop codons by ribosomes. Indeed, when a ribosome encounters a stop codon, translation is either stopped by release factors, or readthrough by a near-cognate tRNA (
i.e.
, making 2 out 3 base pairing with the mRNA codon), which causes protein synthesis to continue beyond the expected termination codon. This specific decoding makes it possible to assess the level of fidelity of the ribosome by measuring the ability of a near-cognate tRNA to be accepted by the ribosome (
28
). Using a dual-reporter plasmid with both β-galactosidase and luciferase coding sequences separated by a single in-frame stop codon (
29
), we compared the readthrough activity of hMEC overexpressing or not ZEB1. We observed that hMEC exhibited a lower percentage of readthrough (around 2%) compared to hMEC-ZEB1 (around 4%) (
Fig. 2
A
), indicating that in hMEC, translation accuracy is higher than in mesenchymal hMEC-ZEB1 cells. Although the RIBOseq phasing is very high, a two-fold increase in readthrough efficiency is not enough to be detected in RIBOseq data.
Fig. 2.
Translational readthrough is higher in ZEB1-induced mesenchymal cells compared to mammary epithelial cells independently of any alteration in the tRNAome. (
A
)
In cellulo

t
test was performed. A significant increase in the percentage of stop codon readthrough was observed in hMEC-ZEB1 compared to hMEC. (
B
) tRNAome. The repertoire of tRNAs was profiled by tRNAseq in epithelial and ZEB1-overexpressing cells. Data are shown as scatter plot (n = 3) and a Pearson’s correlation test was performed. No difference in isodecoders used for stop codon readthrough was observed between the two cell lines. Each differentially expressed tRNA is labeled.
One possibility to increase UGA stop codon readthrough is to overexpress the corresponding near cognate tRNAs that are naturally incorporated at the stop codon (
i.e.
, Trp, Cys, Lys) (
30
). We observed that the increase readthrough efficiency in ZEB1-overexpressing mesenchymal cells were not associated with changes in tRNA expression, as previously described in other conditions (
31
). Using total RNA, tRNAome was compared between hMEC overexpressing or not ZEB1 (
Fig. 2
B
). Only a few significant changes in the tRNA profile were identified impacting different isodecoders, which are not used for stop codon readthrough.
These data demonstrate that readthrough defects are mainly dependent on ribosome activity in our isogenic hMEC cellular models and that ZEB1-induced mesenchymal cells are less efficient and less prone to recognize stop codons than epithelial ones. This observation indicates that mesenchymal ribosomes display remodeling in their intrinsic activity.
Ribosome Composition Is Modified in ZEB1-Induced Mesenchymal Cells at the Ribosomal Protein Level.
Considering the change in translational activity of ZEB1-overexpressing mesenchymal cells, including in translational fidelity, we next investigated changes in ribosome composition. We performed a riboproteome approach,
i.e.
, mass spectrometry (MS)-based quantitative proteomic analysis of purified cytoplasmic ribosomes to highlight any change in the relative amount of ribosomal proteins between hMEC and hMEC-ZEB1 cells (
32
,
33
). Prior to conducting MS-based proteomic characterization, the similarity between protein profiles arising from the five biological replicates of cytoplasmic ribosomes purified from hMEC or hMEC-ZEB1 was verified by 1D SDS-PAGE (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S5
A
and
B
).
MS-based proteomic approach reproducibly identified and quantified more than 900 different proteins in these purified cytoplasmic ribosomes (
Dataset S3
). Nevertheless, using the intensity-based absolute quantification (iBAQ) metrics (
34
), the enrichment in the 80 cytoplasmic ribosomal proteins ranged from 90.7% and 96.4%, demonstrating the high purity of these ribosome preparations. Among the nonribosomal proteins, it appeared that 12 of the 13 subunits of the eIF3 complex were significantly lower in ZEB1-overexpressing hMEC compared to hMEC (
Fig. 3
A
and
SI Appendix
, Fig. S5
C
). Of note, the 13th eIF3 complex subunit, eIF3J, was not identified in our MS-based proteomic dataset, consistently to its description as a labile and nonessential subunit in the mammalian eIF3 complex (
35
). Since a slight increase in the protein levels of each eIF3 subunit was observed in hMEC-ZEB1 compared to hMEC, it indicates that change in riboproteome is not induced by change in gene expression (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S6
). Interestingly, it was previously reported that depletion of the eIF3E subunit promotes EMT commitment, suggesting that our observation may reflect an EMT-dependent remodeling of the eIF3 complex (
21
,
36
).

Among ribosomal proteins, RPL36A alone showed a significant differential abundance in hMEC-ZEB1 compared to hMEC ribosomes (
Fig. 3
A
and
B
). Indeed, a 3-fold increase in the proportion of RPL36A in purified ribosomes was observed in hMEC-ZEB1 compared to hMEC. Of note, MS data cannot discriminate RPL36A from its paralog RPL36AL, which differs from RPL36A by a single amino acid, K38R (UniProt entries: RL36A_HUMAN and RL36L_HUMAN). In the remainder of this section, RPL36A refers to RPL36A and/or RPL36AL. To validate the quantitative proteomic data, we analyzed RPL36A protein levels in both purified ribosomes and ribosome-free fractions by western blot (
Fig. 3
C
and
D
). As expected, ribosomal proteins were detected only in purified ribosome fravctions, and the ribosome-associated factor eIF3E was mostly found in the ribosome-free fractions, where its level was lower in hMEC-ZEB1 compared to hMEC. As for our proteomic data, no change in the RPS6 nor in the RPL19 ribosomal proteins was observed between hMEC and hMEC-ZEB1. However, we confirmed the exclusive and significant increase in RPL36A levels in ribosomes purified from ZEB1-overexpressing mesenchymal cells. Overall, these data suggest that ribosomes of hMEC overexpressing or not ZEB1 exhibit different compositions, the stoichiometry of RPL36A being higher in hMEC-ZEB1 purified ribosomes.
This change in ribosome composition may reflect a change in the total levels of RPL36A in response to ZEB1 overexpression. However, similar levels of total RPL36A mRNA and protein were observed in hMEC-ZEB1 and hMEC (
Fig. 3
E
–
G
). Moreover, no significant difference was observed for RPL36A in our ribosome profiling dataset (
Dataset S1
). These data suggest that the 3-fold increase in the levels of RPL36A in ribosomes purified from ZEB1-overexpressing mesenchymal cells was not linked to similar variation in its protein levels.
Altogether, these data support the existence of ribosome composition remodeling at the protein level in ZEB1-induced mesenchymal cells, which display, at least in part, higher levels of RPL36A in purified ribosomes compared to human mammary epithelial cells.
The Ribosomal Protein RPL36A Triggers EMT.
Before specifically overexpressing a cDNA encoding RPL36A and not RPL36AL to determine whether RPL36A contributes to EMT, we ensured that RPL36A overexpression was associated with the integration of RPL36A within the ribosome using a FLAG-tagged approach. We established a doxycycline-inducible HEK293T cell line overexpressing FLAG-tagged RPL36A, and then purified cytoplasmic ribosomes after 72 h of exposure to 1 µg/mL doxycycline (
Fig. 4
A
and
B
). While no FLAG-tagged protein was detected in HEK293T-RPL36A ribosomes in the absence of doxycycline, HEK293T-RPL36A ribosomes contained a FLAG-tagged protein in response to doxycycline, indicating that FLAG-tagged RPL36A overexpressed proteins were adequately incorporated within the ribosome. Using the immortalized mammary epithelial MCF10A cell line known to undergo EMT (
37
), we independently established three pairs (C2 to C4) of constitutive MCF10A-empty and -RPL36A cell lines using a lentiviral approach and analyzed them 25 d postlentiviral infection. Exogenous
RPL36A
mRNA levels were detected in MCF10A-RPL36A but not in MCF10A-empty clones (
Fig. 4
C
). We then assessed a panel of criteria to determine whether RPL36A is involved in EMT.

First, we observed a change in cell morphology and cell dispersion in response to RPL36A overexpression. Phase contrast imaging showed that MCF10A-RPL36A clones were more isolated and displayed a fibroblast-like morphology compared to MCF10A-empty clones (
Fig. 4
D
). Interestingly, this switch in cell morphology was already observed 11 d after lentiviral infection (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S7
A
–
C
). Using images of Hoechst-stained cells, cell dispersion was quantified using two geometrical models (
i.e.
, Voronoï’s diagram and Delaunay’s triangulation) (
Fig. 5
and
SI Appendix
, Fig. S8
). MCF10A-RPL36A cell lines displayed significantly larger Voronoï areas and longer Delaunay segments than MCF10A-empty cell lines. These two characteristics are features of a greater cell dispersion. These data indicate that RPL36A promotes loss of cell cohesion and acquisition of cell dispersion, a cellular switch usually associated with EMT.

Second, we observed a change in molecular pattern in response to RPL36A overexpression. MCF10A-RPL36A clones expressed lower levels of epithelial markers (CDH1, OCLN, and miR200c) and higher levels of mesenchymal marker (VIM) compared to their paired MCF10A-empty clones, at both mRNA and protein levels, a change supported by immunofluorescent staining (
Figs. 5
A
and
6
and
SI Appendix
, Fig. S7
D
–
F
). In parallel, a significant increase at both mRNA and protein levels in the EMT-TF ZEB1 was observed in response to RPL36A overexpression (
Fig. 6

,
H
, and
I
). Furthermore, MCF10A-RPL36A cell lines expressed significantly higher levels of SNAIL and SLUG proteins compared to MCF10A-empty cell lines; this was associated with a decrease in
SNAI1
mRNA levels but not in
SNAI2
mRNA levels, suggesting a posttranscriptional regulation of SNAI (
Fig. 6

,

Furthermore, since methylation of RPL36A at lysine residues was shown to affect ribosome function, we studied four mutant forms of RPL36A (

Collectively, these data indicate that RPL36A alone specifically promotes a switch in cell morphology, cell dispersion, cell behavior, and molecular pattern. More importantly, RPL36A triggers EMT in the absence of TGF-β, indicating that RPL36A is a strong inducer of EMT by itself.
Discussion
EMT-related cell plasticity is driven by a multilayered regulation of gene expression, in particular transcriptional and epigenetic events (
1
–
3
). To date, some studies have reported a role for translation in reactivating EMT-TF expression and promoting EMT, although no study investigated whether translation is differentially modulated at a genome-wide level in epithelial and mesenchymal cells (
3
). Here, we demonstrated that fine-tuning of the translational landscape and apparatus occurs in mesenchymal mammary cells, the single ribosomal protein RPL36A being sufficient to trigger mammary EMT.
Several years ago, a pioneer study drew the translational landscape of the early phase of a physiologically induced EMT in human heart cells using ribosome profiling (
41
). In response to 45 min of TGF-β treatment, approximately 67 mRNAs were significantly differentially regulated at the translational level, supporting the notion that translational regulation occurs during EMT commitment. However, compared to the numerous data reporting a huge amount of transcriptional and epigenetic changes, this pioneer study suggests only a limited change in translation. Since EMT is a transient and reversible process associated with different metastable stages (
i.e.
, epithelial–mesenchymal plasticity, EMP) (
2
,
42
), we aimed at limiting intra-EMT heterogeneity within the analyzed cell line by first, comparing initial epithelial and final mesenchymal stages and second, using an isogenic model of complete EMT, induced by the overexpression of the EMT-TF ZEB1 in hMEC. Although this ZEB1-induced EMT might be considered nonphysiological, it is stable compared to MCF10A cell line, which displays a high plasticity and therefore, a high intra-EMT heterogeneity (
43
,
44
). As expected, more than 1,000 mRNAs were regulated in our ribosome profiling at steady-state, recapitulating the deep transcriptional reprogramming reported in EMT (
1
,
2
). Unexpectedly, our data revealed a change in translational reprogramming as important as that observed in transcriptional reprogramming; the proportion of mRNAs regulated at these two levels affects 1,000 to 2,000 mRNAs. This notion was supported by two observations. First, similarities and differences in the translational reprogramming induced by two EMT-TFs, ZEB1 and SNAIL, reflected observations made at the transcriptional level and reinforced the fact that these two EMT-TFs induced different EMT programs (
1
,
2
). Second, overrepresentation analysis identified well-known EMT-related biological processes in translationally differentially regulated mRNAs, suggesting that translation contributes to the profound phenotypic changes observed during EMT. Interestingly, the translationally dysregulated mRNAs were involved in biological processes only recently associated with EMT, such as bile acid metabolism or inflammation (
25
–
27
). Thus, translational reprogramming in the field of EMT research could uncover not yet identified biological functions associated with EMT and be a useful approach to characterize and identify EMT heterogeneity (
3
). Altogether, these data reiterate the importance of translational regulation in physiological processes, including in EMT, but also in human diseases, where EMT-induced resistance to cancer therapies has also been shown to rely on translational events (
3
,
45
,
46
).
Several studies recently reported an alteration of the ribosome canonical composition in different pathophysiological contexts, in particular at the level of ribosomal proteins, while it has never been investigated in EMT (
15
,
16
). However, the discovery that mesenchymal cells display the highest readthrough rate, a defect that indicates a modification of translational apparatus (
28
–
30
), supports a modulation of ribosome composition during EMT. Indeed, we identified a change in composition of the ribosome, the level of RPL36A between the mammary epithelial hMEC and mesenchymal hMEC-ZEB1 ribosomes being higher, independently of changes in RPL36A protein levels. Using cryoelectron microscopy (cryo-EM), we could not identify any notable differences in the overall structures of both 80S ribosomes and 60S large subunits from hMEC and hMEC-ZEB1 cells. Both ribosomal populations have the same 1:1 stoichiometry of RPL36A (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S11
). This strongly supports the notion that the increased levels of RPL36A observed in purified ribosomes from ZEB1-induced mesenchymal cells is due to multiple binding sites of RPL36A, some of them being based on dynamic and transitory interactions with the ribosome. Furthermore, a recent study demonstrates that RPL36A is one of the few RPs with the ability to be incorporated into preexisting cytoplasmic ribosomes independently of the canonical ribosome biogenesis (
47
). Indeed, in neurons whose embryonic formation relies on EMT, RPL36A not only shows a short half-life but also exists at substoichiometric levels within the ribosome; its recruitment within the ribosome occurs at a specific subcellular location. Thus, RPL36A has the ability to contribute to heterogeneity of ribosome composition. Overall, these data support the notion that heterogeneity in ribosome composition and in ribosome intrinsic activity are unique molecular features of EMT.
So far, little evidence suggests that ribosomal proteins could contribute to EMT. While ribosomal RPS7 and RPL22L1 proteins were shown to promote a CDH1/VIM switch in prostate and ovarian cancer cell lines, respectively, RPS5 inhibits fibrosis in hepatic stellate cells (
48
–
50
). Interestingly, in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs), two populations of ribosomes coexist, RPL10A- and RPS25-containing ribosomes that actively translate distinct pools of mRNAs, respectively, encoding extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins and B12 vitamin signaling proteins (
51
). Another study revealed a significant enrichment in the translation of profibrotic mRNAs, such as
TIMP1
and
CD90
mRNAs, by purifying RPL10A-associated mRNAs as a surrogate of polysome purification (
i.e.
, actively translated mRNAs) (
52
). Moreover, it has recently been reported that RPL10A-containing ribosomes decrease during mesoderm differentiation, resulting in a decreased translation of mesoderm regulators (
53
). These data identified RPL10A as a specific translational regulator of ECM and mesoderm regulator, which are key EMT markers. Here, using different immortalized mammary MCF10A cell lines, we revealed that RPL36A is a direct inducer of EMT. Indeed, overexpression of RPL36A specifically induced EMT in the absence of the cytokine TGF-β. This conclusion is based on the demonstration that RPL36A overexpression promotes i) a molecular switch, affecting both epithelial/mesenchymal markers and EMT-TFs; ii) the acquisition of a fibroblast-like morphotype, the cells being less cohesive and more dispersed; and iii) a switch in the proliferation/invasion balance; as recommended by the TEMTIA (
2
). Although a loss-of-function experiment would have supported our data, RPL36A knocking-down was ineffective in several cell lines probably due to an autoregulatory loop preventing the induction of cell death through ribosomal stress (
i.e.
, defect in ribosome biogenesis). Moreover, overexpressed FLAG-tagged RPL36A was detected in the ribosome fractions but not in the ribosome-free ones. However, it remains to be demonstrated that RPL36A overexpression affects the stoichiometry of RPL36A in ribosomes purified in MCF10A since RPL36A overexpression drastically slows down their growth, preventing the collection of sufficient cells to purify ribosomes. Of note, the biological function of RPL36A in humans remains under investigation. A single study in a panel of cancer cell lines showed that RPL36A knock-down mostly affects translation compared to transcription, the translationally dysregulated mRNAs being involved in cell cycle, organelle organization, and nucleotide metabolism, that are key cellular functions for EMT commitment (
54
).
Hence, our study demonstrates that a profound translational reprogramming co-occurs with the well-known transcriptional reprogramming in mesenchymal cells. Moreover, it appears that in addition to translation, change in ribosome composition is a unique molecular feature of EMT, as well as a direct inducer of EMT commitment.
Materials and Methods
Cellular Models and Viral Infection.
hMEC line (Lonza Bioscience, CC-2551) and its derivates were cultured in DMEM F12 media (Gibco, 21331020) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (Capricorn Scientific, FBS-12A), 1% penicillin–streptomycin, 0.01 µg/mL hEGF, 0.5 µg/mL hydrocortisone, and 280 mU/mL insulin at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere with 5% CO
2
. MCF10A (ATCC, CRL-10317™) cells were cultured in DMEM F12 media (Gibco, 21331020) supplemented with 5% horse serum (Gibco, 16050122), 1% penicillin–streptomycin, 1X GlutaMax, 2 mM L-Glutamine (Gibco, 25030024), 0.02 µg/mL hEGF, 0.5 µg/mL hydrocortisone, 300 mU/mL insulin, and 100 ng/mL cholera toxin at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere with 5% CO
2
.
Ribosome Profiling and tRNAome.
5.10
7
and 5.10
6
hMEC-derived cells were used for RIBOseq and RNAseq, respectively. Stranded Total RNA library preparation kit respectively (Illumina) and next generation sequencing was performed using a Next Seq single read 75. Data were analyzed using the Ribodoc package (
SI Appendix
,
Materials and Methods
). tRNAome has been realized by Arraystar Inc.
Readthrough Luciferase Reporter Assays.
The pAC18 plasmid (
29
) contains a nonsense mutation (UGA) flanked by two F2A self-cleavage sites that separate the luciferase and β-galactosidase coding phases. β-galactosidase and luciferase activities were assayed using Glo lysis buffer (Promega). Readthrough efficacy was estimated by calculating the ratio of luciferase activity to β-galactosidase activity obtained with the mutant construct, with normalization against an in-frame wild-type control construct.
Ribosome Purification.
Cytoplasmic fractions were obtained by mechanical lysis of cells using the PreCellys device (Ozyme) and centrifugation at 750
g
for 10 min to pellet nuclei then 12,000
g
for 10 min to pellet mitochondria (
32
). Cytoplasmic fractions were loaded onto a 1 M sucrose cushion in buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4; 5 mM MgCl
2
; 500 mM KCl; 2 mM DTT) and centrifuged for 2 h at 250,000
g
. Ribosome pellets were resuspended in buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4; 5 mM MgCl
2
; 25 mM KCl).
MS-Based Quantitative Proteomic Analysis of Ribosomal Fractions.
Five biological replicates of ribosomes were purified from hMEC and hMEC-ZEB1 cell lines before characterization by MS-based proteomic analysis. Only proteins quantified in at least 5 replicates of 1 condition were kept. For each sample, individual iBAQ values were normalized by the sum of iBAQ values coming from ribosomal proteins. Differentially expressed proteins were sorted out using a log2(fold change) cutoff of 1 and an adjusted
P
-value cutoff of 0.005, allowing to reach an FDR threshold of 1% according to the Benjamini–Hochberg estimator.
Immunofluorescence.
Cells were grown on glass coverslips and fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde in 1X PBS before permeabilization with 0.5% Triton X-100 in 1X PBS. Primary antibodies were applied before secondary antibodies were labeled with AlexaFluor488 or 555 (Molecular Probes) (
SI Appendix
, Table S1
). Coverslips were mounted using the Fluoromount G mounting medium (EMS). Images were acquired on a Zeiss confocal microscope (Zeiss LSM780 NLO), thanks to the Cell Imaging Platform (CRCL, Lyon, France).
